articles.title: Mr Olympia 'King Q' cause of death: Dwayne Quamina dies suddenly at 40
articles.standfirst: The Navy veteran had recently urged followers to live without regrets
articles.summary: The Navy veteran had recently urged followers to live without regrets
articles.body:
Less than two weeks separated Dwayne Quamina ’s final bodybuilding appearance from the news that left friends, rivals and fans struggling to comprehend his death.

The 40-year-old Navy veteran, known throughout the sport as “ King Q ,” died suddenly on Sunday after placing sixth in the 212 division at the Atlanta Pro on August 9. No cause of death has been disclosed.

What has made the news especially poignant are the motivational messages Quamina continued sharing almost until the end.

“Stop taking life for granted go all the way and have zero regrets when it’s all over!!” he wrote on Instagram on July 28.

Days before his death, his message was again centered on perseverance.

“If it was easy, everybody would do it,” Quamina wrote. “The best quality you can have is the ability to pick yourself up and go again no matter how many times it take. Watch what comes next!”

Those words now carry a very different weight for the more than 100,000 people who followed his bodybuilding career and online coaching work.

From Navy to the Mr. Olympia stage

Born in Trinidad and Tobago, Quamina later moved to the United States and settled in California. Before bodybuilding became his profession, he spent more than a decade serving in the Navy.

He once described how much that military community meant to him.

“As a veteran, when I got out, the sense of brotherhood is often missed,” Quamina said at a bench press event in El Centro.

Bodybuilding eventually gave him another competitive home. He won the lightweight title at the 2016 NPC USA Championships and followed that by winning the 2017 Europa Phoenix Pro.

His biggest appearance came at the 2018 Mr. Olympia, where he finished 10th in the 212 division.

After stepping away from competition in 2020, Quamina returned in 2025 and placed third at the Chicago Pro before continuing his comeback into 2026. Atlanta became his final contest.

Bodybuilding community rallies around Quamina’s family

The sudden loss has prompted tributes from athletes who had seen Quamina only days earlier.

“No, man, I was just with him last week,” James Hollingshead wrote. Eight-time Ms. Olympia champion Lenda Murray added: “My thoughts and prayers are for the family. Sincere condolences.”

Karol Malecki Ale Lekkie was equally stunned: “It’s absolutely tragic,” he said. “We competed together just a week ago at the Atlanta Pro. It’s hard to believe he’s gone.”

A fundraiser has since been established to support Quamina’s wife, Leah, and their children.

Organizer Keri Valdez described him as “a devoted father, a loving husband, a loyal friend, a proud veteran, and a fitness champion who inspired those around him through his strength, dedication, and determination.”

Only days before his death, Quamina was still speaking about what came next. Now, the messages he left behind have become part of how those closest to bodybuilding are remembering him.

articles.title: Simone Biles proves she’s still the queen of gymnastics with effortless backflip off a yacht
articles.summary: What is learned well is never forgotten, and Simone Biles once again showed why she is considered the best in the world at gymnastics. It doesn’t matter what setting she’s in or how high she has to go—the decorated athlete can still throw a backflip with seemingly little effort and make it look easy. Showing off the technique that has defined her career, Biles was seen performing a backflip off a yacht before landing in the turquoise-blue waters of the sea.

articles.title: WaterMania may be the most surreal wrestling event fans have ever seen
articles.summary: Professional wrestling has never been afraid to embrace the outrageous. Over the decades, fans have seen matches take place in parking lots, graveyards, football stadiums, and even on moving vehicles. Promotions worldwide are constantly searching for new ways to capture attention in an increasingly crowded entertainment landscape. Yet even by wrestling's famously unconventional standards, WaterMania stands in a category of its own. Hosted by French independent promotion Banger Zone Wrestling (BZW), the event features a concept that sounds almost too bizarre to be real: a professional wrestling ring floating in the middle of a swimming pool. The result is one of the most unusual spectacles in modern wrestling—and perhaps one of the most surreal sporting events fans will ever see.

articles.title: WaterMania may be the most surreal wrestling event fans have ever seen
articles.standfirst: Wrestlers must compete while surrounded on all sides by water
articles.summary: Wrestlers must compete while surrounded on all sides by water
articles.body:
Professional wrestling has never been afraid to embrace the outrageous. Over the decades, fans have seen matches take place in parking lots, graveyards, football stadiums, and even on moving vehicles. Promotions around the world are constantly searching for new ways to capture attention in an increasingly crowded entertainment landscape.

Yet even by wrestling's famously unconventional standards, WaterMania stands in a category of its own. Hosted by French independent promotion Banger Zone Wrestling (BZW) , the event features a concept that sounds almost too bizarre to be real: a professional wrestling ring floating in the middle of a swimming pool. The result is one of the most unusual spectacles in modern wrestling, and perhaps one of the most surreal sporting events fans will ever see.

A wrestling ring in the middle of a pool

At first glance, WaterMania looks like something created for a video game rather than a live event. Instead of placing the ring inside a traditional arena, BZW positions it directly in the center of a swimming pool basin. Wrestlers must compete while surrounded on all sides by water, creating an environment where every move carries an added layer of unpredictability.

The setup immediately changes the dynamics of every match. One mistimed step, one powerful throw, or one successful tackle can send competitors tumbling off the ring and into the water below. What might be a routine bump in a conventional wrestling match suddenly becomes a splash-filled spectacle. For fans accustomed to seeing wrestling performed inside ropes surrounded by concrete floors, the visual is unlike anything else in the industry.

Chaos is part of the attraction

WaterMania isn't simply a standard wrestling show with a creative backdrop. The pool itself becomes part of the action. Street fights and other no-disqualification contests often see wrestlers intentionally, or unintentionally, ending up in the water. Competitors use the unique environment to their advantage, creating moments that would be impossible in a traditional venue.

The unpredictability is part of the appeal. In wrestling, fans often know the general rhythm of a match. At WaterMania , however, every exchange carries the possibility of an unexpected plunge into the pool. The setting transforms even familiar wrestling maneuvers into something fresh and entertaining.

The event has developed a reputation as a summer attraction that blends wrestling, festival energy, and pure absurdity. Fans watch from the surrounding pool deck, safely positioned around the basin as spectators rather than participants. Unlike many water-themed events, the audience doesn't have direct access to the pool itself.

Instead, they gather around the perimeter, creating a stadium-like atmosphere around one of the strangest rings in professional wrestling. That unique layout allows spectators to enjoy the action from multiple angles while remaining close enough to feel every splash. The result is an experience that feels part wrestling show, part summer celebration.

articles.title: Simone Biles nearly has a wardrobe malfunction at the US Open
articles.summary: Simone Biles came close to a wardrobe malfunction while making her entrance at the US Open, where the Olympic gymnast walked the Blue Carpet in a chic beige mini skirt and matching sweater. Biles even stopped to congratulate newlywed Paige Paul before the two posed together, but as they chatted, she appeared to realize her skirt was riding up and quickly adjusted it to avoid an awkward moment. The gymnast handled the situation discreetly before continuing down the carpet, greeting fans and guests as if nothing had happened.

articles.title: Simone Biles has a close call with wardrobe malfunction at the US Open
articles.standfirst: The Olympic champion handled the unexpected moment before it turned into an awkward scene
articles.summary: The Olympic champion handled the unexpected moment before it turned into an awkward scene
articles.body:
S It is always good to see Simone Biles supporting her fellow Americans at major competitions , and the Olympic gymnast is no stranger to the US Open. Biles is not only one of the most decorated gymnasts in history, but also an athlete who has paid close attention to fashion as another form of expression.

Now, on the US Open Blue Carpet, that was no exception as Biles arrived in a beige outfit featuring a matching sweater and a short mini skirt. However, the skirt was short enough to nearly cause a wardrobe malfunction during her walk down the carpet.

Biles quickly reacts to the wardrobe scare

Simone Biles, the most decorated gymnast in history and an 11-time Olympic medalist, stopped to congratulate newlywed Paige Paul before the two posed together. As they chatted, Biles appeared to realize that her skirt had ridden up and quickly reacted.

The gymnast discreetly pulled the skirt back down to make sure there was no awkward moment in front of the guests and cameras . She managed to handle the situation without drawing attention to it before continuing her walk down the Blue Carpet and greeting those around her.

Another pressure moment handled by Biles

Biles showed that she knows how to handle pressure not only on the mat , but also when a potential wardrobe malfunction threatens to steal the spotlight at an event.

articles.title: Usain Bolt: "Today I would run the 100 meters in 9.40"'
articles.standfirst: The Jamaican, ambassador of the "Ultimate Championship," points out that he would have liked to race against "Maurice Greene, because he was a showman, and Michael Johnson, because he dominated"
articles.summary: The Jamaican, ambassador of the "Ultimate Championship," points out that he would have liked to race against "Maurice Greene, because he was a showman, and Michael Johnson, because he dominated"
articles.body:
'Usain Bolt, ambassador for World Athletics’ new competition, the "Ultimate Championship" being held in Budapest from this Friday through Sunday, stated that with today’s tracks and the new era of shoes "he would have run somewhat faster than 9.40 in the 100 meters. And in the 200 meters perhaps under 19, a mark I really would have liked to achieve".'

The Jamaican, world record holder in both distances, has just turned 40 and reviewed the current state of international athletics in an interview with "La Gazzetta". In that regard, Bolt highlighted that "apart from my distances, I always passionately follow the 800 meters, which are now almost a sprint race, and the 110-meter hurdles. Then I think the javelin throw should be valued more, since its protagonists are true phenomena".

Except for my distances, I always follow the 800 meters with passion, which is now almost a sprint race

In addition, he stated that from another era he would have liked to compete against "Maurice Greene, because he was a showman, and Michael Johnson, because he dominated", while from today "there are so many, and not to offend anyone, I will mention some of my compatriot sprinters: Oblique Seville, world champion in the 100 meters, and the twins Tia and Tina Clayton".

“Will my records be broken? Not soon, I don’t see anyone capable. But I have two children...”

Bolt would advise young Usain to work harder: I was wrong to think that talent was enough. If I had believed that, my first Olympic Games, Athens 2004, would have been different". And regarding the fact that they call him a legend, he emphasized that "it means being on the same level as champions like Muhammad Ali and Pelé: an extraordinary effect".

As for his records, the former Jamaican sprinter believes they are still not in danger: "Not soon, I don't see anyone capable. But I have two children..." And he leaves the robot races for show. "Fun, but they didn't excite me too much."

articles.title: Hyrox will review its rules after allowing the world champion to compete covered in feces in Beijing
articles.standfirst: Joanna Wietrzyk, the current world champion, suffered sudden bowel incontinence while competing, but she finished the race and took first place
articles.summary: Joanna Wietrzyk, the current world champion, suffered sudden bowel incontinence while competing, but she finished the race and took first place
articles.body:
The German company Hyrox , organizer of the sports competition that attracts thousands of people around the world, will review its rules after the scandal caused this weekend in Beijing by an Australian athlete who was allowed to finish the race despite being covered in feces.

Joanna Wietrzyk, the current world champion in her category, suffered sudden stomach incontinence on Saturday while competing, but she finished the race and took first place. The incident, which has gone viral on social media , has caused outrage among numerous fans of the discipline and editorials in specialized media outlets, which believe that in an event where spitting on the track or pouring water over oneself is penalized, the athlete received special treatment because of her elite status and because she is sponsored by Puma, which is also an official sponsor of Hyrox.

Wietrzyk later posted a photo of herself on a medical stretcher on Instagram with the text "a win is a win", but she later deleted it, though not before receiving hundreds of comments questioning her sportsmanship and reproaching her for not withdrawing so as not to put the health of the rest of the participants and venue staff at risk.

"As our sport evolves, we encounter new and increasingly complex situations that pose a challenge and in which greater clarity is needed," says a statement from the franchise issued this Monday, which also states that Hyrox "applies clear medical and biocontamination protocols".

The statement says that what happened last Saturday in the Chinese capital was "an unexpected situation in which the protocols designed for elite competition and mass participation competition became blurred, creating ambiguity in how they were understood and applied."

"We recognize that this can, naturally, cause frustration, questions, and heated opinions within our community. Those concerns are legitimate and, as organizers, we must be prepared to listen to them, investigate what happened, and hold ourselves accountable so we can continue improving," it adds.

The company also issued a stern warning after Wietrzyk allegedly received threats online and said it is investigating and will ban those responsible from attending future events.

A participant who competed on the day of the incident and witnessed what happened live told EFE that the situation was exactly as shown in the images circulating on social media: the athlete suffered severe incontinence less than halfway through the race but remained in the competition, leaving feces on the running track as she went and on the equipment, machines, and mats shared with the rest of the athletes.

"The cleaning was not carried out at that moment , but rather at the end of the day, and there were people who got soiled and even slipped on the feces," the witness said.

The Chinese state-run newspaper Global Times also reported on the controversy this Monday, quoting sports commentator Zhu Meng: " True sportsmanship is about knowing where to draw the line , because competition should never continue at the expense of public health and the rights of other athletes," he said.

Likewise, Chinese social media has reacted with indignation, questioning why the organizers and the medical team did not act in time, while participants from that same day said that the proper course of action would be for Hyrox to refund the money—about $150 per participant—to the people who competed at the same time as the Australian woman and were exposed to health risks.

Hyrox is a sports competition created in 2017 that alternates eight kilometers of running with eight strength exercises, with the goal of completing it in the shortest possible time. It is held in venues in more than 20 countries, and its franchise was valued at more than 600 million euros by the end of 2025, according to Forbes magazine.

articles.title: Shavarsh Karapetyan, an unsung hero who saved 20 lives: “Heroism isn't a gift; it's a choice”
articles.standfirst: The Armenian man saved the lives of about twenty people who had fallen from a trolleybus into the icy waters of Lake Yerevan. The rescue led to sepsis
articles.summary: The Armenian man saved the lives of about twenty people who had fallen from a trolleybus into the icy waters of Lake Yerevan. The rescue led to sepsis
articles.body:
This is an interview with a hero. It happened 50 years ago, on this very day. Shavarsh Karapetyan was 23 years old and was a world legend in fin swimming. He had won several titles and held several records. A trolleybus carrying 90 passengers plunged from the dike into Lake Yerevan , in Armenia , then part of the Soviet Union . Shavarsh had just finished training with his brother Kamo , a 20 km run along the shore. He heard a deafening crash and saw the vehicle sink 25 meters into murky, freezing water. He tells the rest himself, with the help of his daughter Zara, who serves as translator.

Question . What do you remember about the exact instant you decided to jump into the water without thinking twice?

Answer . I remember everything, and I remember nothing. The sound — it was like a bomb exploding. The dust, the mist, the screams. I was finishing a brutal 20-kilometer run with my brother Kamo, carrying weights on my back. We were about 25 meters away. I didn't decide to jump. My body moved before my mind could catch up. It was pure instinct. But I also remember one thing clearly: I turned to the other young men and forbade them to enter the water. I allowed only my brother to stay on the surface to take people from me. I told myself — if something happens to me, my parents will still have him. I knew I could hold my breath for six minutes. I knew my limits. So I jumped. There was no hesitation. There was no time for fear. There were people dying, and I was the only one who could reach them. And also, I understood that if I lost consciousness, only my brother Kamo would be able to pull me out, because he was also a finswimmer. I clearly understood that if we worked as a team — him on the surface, me underwater — we could save more people than if we both dove together and exhausted our strength at the same time. But all of this happened in a matter of seconds, and most likely, what worked in that moment was the fact that I am the older brother and I carry responsibility for the younger one.

Q. How did you manage to orient yourself and act so precisely underwater, in murky water where you couldn't see anything?

Zero visibility. Complete darkness. The silt had risen from the bottom, and the water was black like ink. I couldn't see my own hand in front of my face. So I stopped relying on my eyes. I relied on my hands — on feeling. I dove down ten meters, again and again. I broke the back window with my legs — the glass cut me deeply, but pain was irrelevant. I went inside through that broken window. I searched in the darkness. I touched bodies, I grabbed arms, I pulled people out. It was like being in a nightmare. But I was trained for the water. I knew how to stay calm. I knew how to control my breathing. And I knew that every second I wasted, someone died. So I didn't waste a single one. God did not send just a man who can swim to that place. He sent a finswimmer — someone who knows exactly how to work underwater and how to control his breathing.

Q. At what point did you feel your body reaching its physical limit?

I don't remember how many dives I made. My body was already exhausted from the run. The water was cold — maybe 12 or 13 degrees Celsius. My lungs were burning. My legs were cramping. But the true moment I felt my limit was not when I was exhausted. It was when I surfaced on one of my last dives, completely out of oxygen, almost losing consciousness — and I realized I was holding a leather bus seat in my hands. Not a person. I had grabbed a seat instead of a human being. I could have saved someone else. That moment — the realization that I had made a mistake, that I might have cost a life — that was my true limit. I still dream about that seat sometimes. I still regret it.

Q. You suffered sepsis and serious lung damage from the contaminated water. How did that change your athletic career and your daily life afterward?

The doctors told me I was very close to being taken directly from the shore to the morgue. I spent 45 days in intensive care with double pneumonia and blood poisoning. The sepsis nearly killed me. After a month and a half, I forced myself to stand up. I went back to training. I was not going to let it end like that. In my next competition, I set my last world record. But my lungs were destroyed. The disease eventually won, and I was forced to leave big sport. It changed everything. I couldn't train at the same level. I couldn't push myself the way I used to. But I never complained. I made a choice, and I paid the price willingly. That is what it means to be a man. A person with damaged lungs cannot continue training. No one thought I could set another record — let alone even swim. They didn't believe I could do it. But leaving like that — it was not the Karapetyan way. I set a goal: to break my own last record and leave as a winner. My guardian angel — the same one who told me to be at that place and save those people — also saved me and helped me leave big sport as a champion.

Q. Did your country help you after that episode?

These were not easy times for Armenia. Armenia was just becoming what it is today. And I am the kind of person who believes that there is no heroism in this at all — it is simply a duty. And I am sure that every Armenian would have done the same thing.

In 1982, six years later, an article was published about me. Only then did I receive 60,000 letters from people all over the Soviet Union. But I did not do it for recognition. I did it because people were dying. And I would do it again, even if nobody ever knew my name.

Q. Did you ever feel that the physical price you paid was "too high," or did you never doubt it?

I never doubted it. Not once. I knew the risks. I knew I was sacrificing my body. But let me tell you something important. On that day, I was supposed to be in Hanover, Germany, for the World Championship. But I was not included in the team. It hurt me deeply. So I returned to Yerevan and went to train at the lake. If I had been in Hanover, those 20 people would have died. I believe I was meant to be there. I believe a higher power put me there. So no — the price was not too high. It was exactly what was required. As my father always said, and as I have always believed: in this life, we all owe everything to each other.

Q. Could you tell me about your childhood?

I had three brothers. We all did sports, and we all swam. But swimming was not my first love. When I was a child, my parents sent me to gymnastics. I wanted to be like the Olympic champion in gymnastics — Albert Azaryan. He was my hero. I trained hard. I set a goal for myself to reach great heights. I dreamed of it.

But then, some time passed, and the coach called my father. He told him: "You need to take the boy out of gymnastics. He has nothing. He will not succeed." It was like a punch to the chest. I was devastated. My father was devastated too. For little Shavarsh, it was a real shock. I had set my goal so high, I had believed so strongly — and then I was told I was not good enough. It broke my heart.

So I left gymnastics. I was lost for a while. And then I ended up in swimming by chance... completely by accident. But in the end, as you already understand, it was not a coincidence at all. It was destiny. It was written. What seemed like failure was actually the universe pushing me toward my true path. So now I know: sometimes rejection is redirection. Sometimes losing one dream opens the door to a greater one. That is what happened to me. I learned early that discipline and hard work are not punishments — they are the foundation of everything.

What about my parents? My parents gave me love, but they also gave me responsibility. And I am grateful for that. Because without that foundation, I would not have been able to do what I did later.

Q. You were a world champion finswimmer, but the world remembers you for that day at the reservoir. How do you live with your heroism overshadowing your sporting achievements?

I am proud of my medals. Seventeen world championships. Thirteen European championships. Eleven world records. Those are the results of years of blood, sweat, and sacrifice. But those are titles. What happened on that day at the reservoir was something else — it was a human duty. It does not overshadow my career. It is simply a different part of my life. I often say that anyone can find themselves in a place where somebody needs help. The main thing is not to forget what makes you human. My sporting achievements belong to me. That day at the reservoir belongs to everyone. You are wrong to think that this incident overshadows my sporting achievements. I am a Soviet man. I grew up and became a champion in the Soviet Union. My country was proud of this fact. My parents were proud. And I was proud too.

Q. Does the label of "hero" make you uncomfortable, or do you accept it naturally?

I feel like a man who saw a disaster and reacted. There is a story I like to tell. A group of schoolchildren once formed a society called "Shavarshevtsy" — they dedicated themselves to helping elderly people. They said: "A true hero stays unknown for a long time, like Shavarsh." I was moved by that. But still, I don't wear the word "hero" easily. Because when people call you a hero, they sometimes forget that you are human. They forget that you make mistakes. They forget that you feel pain. I accept it only because I know it comes from love. But inside, I am just a man who did what any man should do.

Q. Do you believe an elite athlete's training — discipline, the ability to endure suffering, staying calm under pressure — was decisive in being able to act that way?

Absolutely. Without my training, I could not have done it. My sport — finswimming — is not just swimming. It is power training, running, and most importantly, breathwork. Learning to hyperventilate. Learning to hold my breath for six minutes. Learning to stay calm in the water under extreme pressure. When I was underwater, I was in my element. My pain tolerance, my ability to endure suffering, my discipline — all of that was honed by years of brutal training. It was not bravery. It was mechanics. It was the reaction of a professional who knew exactly what his body could do. I always tell young athletes: train hard, because you never know when your training will be needed for something greater than sport.

Q. If you could speak to someone today who hesitates to act in an emergency, what would you tell them?

I would say: do not ask yourself if you can. Ask yourself who you are. We are all born as human beings. If you see suffering and you hesitate, then what separates you from the animals? It is not about fear. It is about love. In difficult moments like that, love for your fellow humans grows stronger than fear. If you know you can help, you must help. Otherwise, you cannot call yourself a man. I have lived my whole life by one simple rule: when you see someone in trouble, you don't think — you act. That is what makes us human.

But at the same time, it is stupid to jump in and save someone without assessing your own strength. You should not do that. You must know your limits. You must be honest with yourself. If you cannot help, do not become another victim. That helps no one. So yes — act. But act with your head as well as your heart.

Q . Over the years, has the way you understand what you did that day changed?

No. I have never changed my understanding. I know I did what had to be done. But I do think sometimes about the "what ifs." What if I had been a few seconds faster? What if I had made fewer mistakes? Could I have saved more? but I still think about the ones I didn't save. That feeling does not change. It stays with you forever. But I also understand now, more than before, that I was not acting alone. I was guided by something bigger than myself. And I am at peace with that.

Q. Is there something about that experience you wish people understood, that usually doesn't get told?

Yes. I want people to understand that I am not a superhuman. I am a man. I paid for that day with my health and my career — yes. But the true cost is the memory and human life. Nothing is worth more than a human life: not cars, not apartments, not pedigree, not even airplanes. You take nothing with you to the other world. The most important thing is human life.

I want people to understand: heroism is not a gift. It is a decision. A decision that anyone can make. We just have to be ready for it. And we must be ready not for glory, but for sacrifice. That is the part that usually does not get told. And that is the part that matters most.
